Edit: "Reasons We Share Personal Data" is what people are talking about, not Windows 10 specific policies. They do actually have to believe it's necessary to have specific files to comply with the law. They can't just bulk collect based on this section.

Let's break down what the official page on Windows 10 privacy says (the one linked to from the user agreement):

Activation: totally fine, only sends activation key if necessary.

Advertising ID: easy to opt-out, same practice as other advertising companies

Input Personalization: "You can turn off Input Personalization at any time. This will stop the data collection for this feature and will delete associated data stored on your device"

Location Services: Send location info to MS, but can easily be turned off.

Security and Safety features:

--Device Encryption: Bitlocker key is automatically backed up on OneDrive. 2 reasons this is not an issue: 1, it doesn't mean sending the data on the hdd to MS, it only means sending the key. A key is useless without the data. 2, if you are a target for law enforcement, a key won't stop the gov't from forcing you to enter the key. In short, no problems caused by this.

--Malware Removal Tool: "If you do not want MSRT to send this data to Microsoft, you can disable MSRT's reporting component. "

--Microsoft Family: Essentially, MS data mining this is the parents fault. MS is only giving the option to track.

--SmartScreen: SmartScreen can be turned off, but the data sending to MS is necessary to check the program without having a huge database on the PC wasting space.

--Defender: same deal as Malware Removal Tool

Sync Settings: only applies to MS accounts, MS accounts can still disable a lot

Telemetry: If set to basic, MS gets the PC specs, what is installed (so they know if you have Tor if it's installed, but not what you do on it), and if your PC is working correctly (yes-no, not a huge concern). Enhanced sees how often you use said programs, but not what you do on them. Full gets system files, so and memory snapshots. This is only if a program crashes, but it could contain stuff you were doing when it crashed, but not your documents on your HDD.

--Error Reporting: This will however send "files that help describe the problem." This is a little broad, but error means an accident, so something you accessed on purpose could not be considered an "error," and it would only be files that "describe the problem" so they can't just get bank statements if MS word crashed, unless you happened to have your finances in the word document.

Updates: Essentially just installs new fixes and possibly new software, however this software still has to comply with the privacy policy, so it is not worrisome. People should be updating their PCs anyway, so I think this is a step in the right direction.

Edge and IE: only new privacy issues are if you have Cortana, Page predictions, or suggested sites, otherwise after disabling this, privacy is the same as any browser except for the lack of extensions (lack of extensions is a big one, but it's not MS's fault since it was rushed)

Wifi Sense: If MS has your wifi, as long as you have HTTPS, MS can't just use a snoop beacon to catch your traffic. Wifi passwords are not actually that big of an issue. It's not necessarily what MS does, but whatever friends do on the network. IP related liability is pretty low, otherwise hola users would be in trouble, and there has not been a single criminal case against an hola user. I don't think it's anything to worry about (heck I have an open hotspot, it really doesn't matter much)

Windows apps: all can be turned off through privacy panel

Windows Hello: opt-in, requires special hardware anyway

Store: no privacy issues, but walled gardens suck, and it's littered with ads, so stay away anyway.
